tldr: We introduce SymmGrid, a trajectory-level augmentation framework that massively amplifies data by applying grid-like parallelized symmetric transformations directly during on-robot reinforcement learning. In real-robot, contact-rich manipulation tasks, it speeds up wall-clock training convergence by 1.37–2.17x compared to the state-of-the-art method (SERL), achieving policy convergence in as little as 10.9 minutes.
hero_caption: The three contact-rich real-robot manipulation tasks evaluated in this work using a Franka Research 3 (FR3) robot. From left to right: high-precision peg insertion, cable routing involving a deformable object, and an object relocation task moving a compliant ball between trays where grasping and contact conditions vary easily.
overview:
On-robot learning, where reinforcement learning is run directly on physical robots, is an ideal approach because it bypasses the simulation-to-real gap (Sim2Real gap) and learns real-world contact physics firsthand. However, the biggest hurdle is slow training in real wall-clock time. Even state-of-the-art approaches require tens of minutes to several hours to train a single policy, hindering rapid deployment to real-world environments.

To tackle this, the authors turned their attention to the underlying spatial symmetries (translational symmetries) of physical phenomena. Drawing inspiration from biological branching structures (such as racemose inflorescences), they devised SymmGrid, a framework that takes a single collected trajectory (a sequence of states and actions) and applies parallel affine transformations that translate the entire space. By applying transformations across a 27×27 grid, for instance, a single real-world trial is super-scaled into 729 times as many equivalent and valid transition data points poured into the replay buffer (memory storing experiences).

Evaluations across three challenging tasks using a physical Franka arm—peg insertion, cable routing, and compliant object relocation—demonstrated that SymmGrid reduced training convergence time by 1.37–2.17x compared to the baseline SERL. In particular, it reached high success rates in just 10.9 minutes for cable routing and 16.6 minutes for peg insertion, bringing real-world robot reinforcement learning much closer to the sub-10-minute regime.
contributions: Proposed SymmGrid, an RL framework that applies constant-branching parallelized symmetric transformations at the trajectory level to super-scale real-world interaction data onto geometric grids.

Engineered a mechanism that preserves visual invariance with minimal memory and compute overhead by applying projective transformations (homographies) at sampling time for static fixed cameras (exocentric view) as well as wrist-mounted cameras (egocentric view).

Demonstrated 1.37–2.17x wall-clock training speedups and up to 1.27x evaluation success rate improvements over the state-of-the-art SERL across physical peg-insertion, cable routing, and compliant object relocation tasks.

sections.heading: Breaking through the real-robot RL training bottleneck with spatial symmetry
sections.summary: While deep reinforcement learning directly on physical robots captures real contact physics, lengthy training times remain a major bottleneck for practical deployment. SymmGrid massively amplifies data through parallelized symmetries inspired by biological branching, enabling task mastery in just 10-odd minutes.
sections.details:
On-robot reinforcement learning, where robots learn directly in the physical world, is uniquely compelling for contact-rich, complex manipulation. It directly handles physical nuances like friction and deformation that simulators struggle to capture accurately. However, even current state-of-the-art (SOTA) approaches require 20 to 180 minutes of physical robot operational time, even after being seeded with around 20 human demonstrations.

Physical laws harbor symmetries, and prior research has explored utilizing them to boost learning efficiency. Yet, earlier symmetry approaches were held back because they could only extract a very limited set of transformation patterns. SymmGrid addresses this by expanding space across a grid following regular rules, reminiscent of plant branching, generating hundreds of symmetric equivalences from a single experience.

For the wrist camera (egocentric view), translating the robot preserves the relative view between the gripper and the object, allowing memory-efficient pointer referencing. For the fixed camera (exocentric view), applying homographies (planar projective transformations) on the fly during sampling maintains geometric consistency without blowing up memory. As a result, the method achieved unprecedented convergence speeds on physical robots, reaching task completion in as fast as 10.9 minutes.

sections.heading: Prior approaches to symmetry versus SymmGrid's 'super-scaling'
sections.summary: Earlier works integrated reflection or rotation symmetries into action-value functions or network architectures, but were constrained to a small number of transformations. SymmGrid uses fractal-inspired branching structures to scale symmetric transformations by orders of magnitude.
sections.details:
Incorporating symmetries into reinforcement learning has a rich history. Here is a look at how key prior works approached this:

- Leveraging reflection symmetry: ITER flipped state-action pairs, achieving several-fold improvements in sample efficiency across simulated reach and slide tasks.
- Embedding rotational symmetries into networks: Methods have leveraged cyclic groups ($C_{12}$) or dihedral groups ($D_4$) to give convolutional neural networks rotation equivariance (where rotating the input rotates the output correspondingly).
- Equivariant reinforcement learning: Frameworks like Equi-SAC embedded SO(2) rotational symmetry into the Q-function to learn grasping and pushing on physical UR5 robots, but convergence still took between 45 minutes and 2 hours 40 minutes.

Crucially, these prior works were limited by using only a small handful of symmetric transformations. SymmGrid departs decisively by adopting a flexible branching structure that generates hundreds of transformations all at once (super-scaling). By translating the concept of fractal symmetry from preliminary work into a practical constant grid, the authors demonstrated substantial gains in real-robot, vision-based manipulation setups.

sections.heading: Plant geometry, Markov decision processes, and the SERL baseline
sections.summary: This section covers the mathematical foundations behind the approach: branching geometry via iterated function systems (IFS), continuous-space Markov Decision Processes (MDPs), and the state-of-the-art robot RL suite SERL used as the baseline.
sections.details:
Three fundamental components form the foundation of this method:

- Branching systems: Plants in nature (especially those with corymb-like inflorescences) build efficient architectures by repeating simple geometric rules. Iterated function systems (IFS) formalize this mathematically. Nodes are expanded via affine transformations (combinations of translations and rotations) to define a $K \times K$ two-dimensional grid structure.
- Markov Decision Processes (MDPs): The standard RL setup is defined over a continuous state space $\mathcal{S}$, action space $\mathcal{A}$, unknown transition dynamics $\mathcal{P}$, and a reward function $R$. The goal is learning a stochastic policy $\pi_\theta$ that maximizes expected cumulative reward with entropy regularization.
- The baseline SERL: An efficient off-policy RL framework that builds around RLPD (Reinforcement Learning with Prior Data). SERL leverages asynchronous training, compliance via impedance control, and dual replay buffers (separating demonstration and online data) to achieve state-of-the-art wall-clock speeds (36 to 105 minutes). SymmGrid uses SERL's environments and configurations as its direct baseline for comparison.

sections.heading: The mechanics of branched MDPs: cloning entire trajectories across a grid
sections.summary: By applying global translational affine transformations across entire executed trajectories, SymmGrid generates vast numbers of equivalent trajectories while preserving rewards and dynamics. On a 27×27 grid, a single step explodes into 729 valid data points.
sections.details:
The core insight behind SymmGrid is reframing a contact-rich trajectory $\tau = \langle s_0, a_1, r_1, s_1, \dots \rangle$ as vertices (states) and edges (actions) within a tree structure.

The transformation $\sigma$ used here is a global translation. It adds a constant spatial offset $t_k$ to state components $s$, such as the end-effector position coordinates. Because relative end-effector action commands $a$ and resulting rewards $r$ are preserved, physically consistent new trajectories are synthesized instantly. In essence, it exploits the symmetry that executing the exact same relative task somewhere else in space is physically equivalent.

Specifically, a square 'Symmetry Workspace' (SymWS) is defined around the robot end-effector, and $K \times K$ grid points are distributed across it in parallel. For $K=27$, a single original trajectory yields 729 valid trajectories that are immediately loaded into the replay buffer.

Handling image data efficiently is crucial here. Since translations do not alter the view seen by an egocentric wrist camera, buffer entries point to the same original image via pointers to prevent memory bloat. For evaluation, the paper measures performance not just by final success rates, but through normalized area under the curve (nAUC) ratios across learning curves to capture both initial sample efficiency and learning stability.

sections.heading: Correcting fixed camera shifts smartly with homographies
sections.summary: Fixed external cameras see objects shift as the end-effector moves. SymmGrid preserves geometric consistency without exhausting memory by applying planar projective transformations (homographies) on the fly during mini-batch sampling.
sections.details:
Unlike wrist cameras, a fixed external camera (exocentric view) viewing the workspace will capture a different visual scene if the robot operates at a different location. Naively applying symmetric coordinate shifts would create inconsistencies with the recorded images.

To solve this, the framework uses homographies (planar projective transformations). A calibration matrix $M$ mapping workspace plane coordinates to image pixel coordinates is determined in advance, allowing the transformation matrix $H_b(\Delta) = M T_b(\Delta) M^{-1}$ for spatial translation $\Delta$ to be precomputed.

Two key implementation strategies make this practical:
- Precomputing inverse mappings: To avoid holes or artifacts in transformed images, the backward mapping from output pixels to input pixels is established once at initialization.
- On-the-fly transformations at sampling time: Storing transformed images for every grid point would exhaust storage and memory. Instead, the replay buffer only records the index identifying which transformation was applied. When a mini-batch is sampled during training, `remap()` is applied to the base image on the fly.

For pixels shifted outside image boundaries, edge pixel replication is used rather than solid color padding, minimizing negative impacts on visual representation encoders.

sections.heading: Real Franka evaluations: 10-minute convergence and emergent behaviors
sections.summary: Tested across peg insertion, cable routing, and compliant object relocation, SymmGrid reduced convergence time by up to 2.17x over SERL, reaching a 98% success rate in as fast as 10.9 minutes. The robot also developed diverse emergent behaviors, including unanticipated push and drag tactics.
sections.details:
Experiments were run on a physical Franka Research 3 (FR3) arm against the SERL baseline. The policy processes visual inputs with a ResNet-10 backbone and outputs target 6D/7D end-effector deltas through a 2-layer MLP.

- Peg insertion task: Using two wrist cameras, SymmGrid ($K=27$) converged to a 100% training success rate in an average of 18.5 minutes (fastest at 14.77 minutes), delivering a 1.41x speedup (a 28.8% reduction in clock time) over SERL (average 26 minutes). Evaluation success hit 100% in 16.6 minutes (Figure F3).
- Cable routing task: A demanding contact task threading a flexible cable into brackets. SymmGrid achieved a 98% evaluation success rate in just 10.9 minutes (1.27x faster than SERL). While SERL plateaued around an average of 74.8% after 25 minutes, SymmGrid consistently maintained over 98% success (Figure F4).
- Compliant object relocation task: Combining one wrist camera and one fixed camera, the robot transfers a soft knitted ball between trays. Incorporating homographies, SymmGrid converged to 92% accuracy in 79.3 minutes (SERL required 130 minutes). At 10,000 steps, evaluation success reached 99.3%, well ahead of SERL's 74.7% (Figure F6).

Qualitative observations revealed several emergent strategies due to ball compliance: pushing with outer fingers, dragging from inner surfaces, pinch-sliding, and standard pinching (Figure F7). The policy remained resilient even when the camera was briefly obstructed or the tray was tilted up to 30 degrees.

captions.F3: Comparison of training curves (left) and evaluation success rates (right) on the peg insertion task. The green SymmGrid curve rises noticeably faster than the red SERL baseline, reaching nearly 100% success around the 15-minute mark.
captions.F4: Results on the deformable cable routing task. SymmGrid (green) climbs sharply around 10 minutes, quickly reaching high precision (over 98%) that SERL (red) could not match even after 25 minutes.
captions.F6: Forward model training curves on the object relocation task with an exocentric camera. SymmGrid with a narrower workspace (0.175 m) and 3 branches (dark green) significantly outperforms SERL (red), achieving over 90% accuracy.
captions.F7: Emergent robot behaviors observed during the compliant ball relocation task. From left to right: outer finger pushing, inner finger dragging, pinch-pushing, and standard pinch grasping, illustrating flexible contact strategies adapted to conditions.

sections.heading: Why it works, and the limits of scaling with exocentric cameras
sections.summary: Learning global geometric symmetries drastically accelerates adaptation to local contact dynamics. However, applying homographies to fixed camera images exposed clear trade-offs, where parallax and border artifacts degrade data quality if scaled too aggressively.
sections.details:
The key reason SymmGrid accelerates learning so dramatically is that it lets the robot quickly absorb the global geometric structure of the workspace from parallel data. This frees the model to concentrate its capacity on learning subtle local contact physics. In the object relocation task, this saved over 35 minutes of physical robot time, making practical on-robot training far more viable.

At the same time, the experiments highlighted clear trade-offs. While peg insertion and cable routing (wrist cameras only) benefited from large $27 \times 27$ grids, object relocation using a fixed camera performed best with a smaller setup: 3 branches ($3 \times 3$) and a modest 0.175 m workspace width.

Why does aggressive scaling backfire with fixed cameras? Real workspaces feature multiple depth planes—the table, trays, and the arm itself. Projecting these scenes using a single planar homography inevitably introduces parallax distortion and edge artifacts. Generating too many transformations floods the replay buffer with visual inconsistencies, leading the neural network to overfit to unnatural distortions rather than true underlying task geometry.

sections.heading: Conclusion: moving toward sub-10-minute on-robot learning
sections.summary: Combining simple translational affine transformations with branching structures breaks previous speed limits in physical robot reinforcement learning. This represents an important milestone toward acquiring real contact physics directly on hardware in minutes.
sections.details:
This work presented SymmGrid, a framework that super-scales spatial translational symmetries across geometric grids to augment reinforcement learning replay buffers. Despite relying on straightforward global transformations, tailoring implementations to sensor perspectives—pointer referencing for egocentric wrist cameras and on-the-fly homographies for exocentric fixed cameras—delivered 1.37–2.17x convergence speedups on physical hardware.

Simulating complex contact dynamics like deformable cables or compliant balls remains difficult. Enabling physical robots to learn these behaviors directly in roughly 10 to 20 minutes from scratch provides a valuable framework for deploying manipulators and humanoid robots in the real world.

takeaways: Applying global translational symmetries to entire trajectories dramatically boosts sample and wall-clock efficiency in contact-rich physical robot RL.
Because egocentric wrist camera views remain invariant under translations, pointer referencing enables hundred-fold data augmentation without increasing memory footprints.
Exocentric fixed camera images can be adapted via homographies during sampling, but branching factors and workspace bounds require careful tuning to limit parallax and border artifacts.
Reaching policy convergence in around 10 minutes compared to state-of-the-art SERL brings direct on-robot reinforcement learning much closer to practical real-world deployment.
limitations: Homography transformations on fixed exocentric cameras assume planar surfaces, causing parallax distortions in scenes with pronounced depth variations that can hinder learning if augmented excessively.
Evaluated symmetric transformations are currently restricted to pure 2D translations along the base frame's xy-plane, without fully exploiting 3D rotations or broader geometric symmetry groups.
Initializing policies still requires collecting roughly 20 to 30 manual human demonstrations for behavioral cloning priors.
